theme: Atlas Freight platform engineering keeps its handbook, runbook, incident and planning notes in one HedgeDoc instance

credentials.admin: admin@tester-env.local / HedgeDocAdmin2026! (owner: onboarding checklist, API style guide, Q4 hiring plan)
credentials.dana: dana@tester-env.local / HedgeDocDana2026! (owner: release runbook, postmortem, weekly sync, 1:1 notes)
credentials.priya: priya@tester-env.local / HedgeDocPriya2026! (no owned notes; history only)

seed_command: ./tester-env seed (tester-env-seed.js seed; safe to re-run on a seeded instance)
verify_command: ./tester-env verify (health, three logins, every note page, the permission matrix, rendered markdown, revision lists and history entries)
notes: Notes are created through POST /new/<alias> with fixed aliases, then permissions, owners, last-change times and revisions are written through the app's own Sequelize models: HedgeDoc exposes no HTTP route for permissions, revision contents or timestamps. Notes.createdAt is pinned with one UPDATE because Sequelize ignores createdAt on instance updates.

History entries are written through POST /history with a fixed JSON array per user (note id, title, millisecond time, pinned flag, tags), so /history and its pin/tag results are stable without socket.io.
Seed deletes and recreates only the eight notes and the history of the three users it owns, so re-running seed leaves exactly one copy of every seeded record and keeps unrelated notes.

Every date is absolute and fixed (notes 2026-08-11 .. 2026-11-20, history entries 2026-10-30 .. 2026-11-21); nothing is derived from the wall clock. /history renders relative 'fromNow' text, so assert order/pinned/tags rather than that text.
Published-view requests (/s/<alias>) increment viewcount, so view counts are not part of the stable inventory; verify excludes them.
Note ids, shortids and publish shortids are generated by HedgeDoc; assertions key on aliases, titles, permissions, counts, lengths, dates and rendered text.

TZ=UTC in docker-compose.tester-env.yml. Anonymous access, anonymous edits and free-URL aliases are enabled; email registration is disabled, so the three accounts come from deploy (admin) and the seed (dana, priya).

admin-login.evidence: deploy creates admin@tester-env.local / HedgeDocAdmin2026! through bin/manage_users; verify logs in through POST /login and requires the signed-in index (/logout).

multi-user-roles.evidence: Three accounts with fixed passwords: admin (3 owned notes), dana (4 owned notes), priya (no owned notes). verify logs in as each; the note permission matrix differs per account.

populated-note-list.evidence: 8 notes with stable aliases and titles: engineering-onboarding, release-runbook, api-style-guide, q4-hiring-plan, postmortem-dispatch-latency, weekly-sync-2026-11-17, platform-glossary, one-to-one-dana. Every page renders its title and the editor shell.

permission-variety.evidence: All six HedgeDoc permissions are represented: freely (platform-glossary), editable (engineering-onboarding, weekly-sync-2026-11-17), limited (release-runbook), locked (api-style-guide), protected (postmortem-dispatch-latency), private (q4-hiring-plan, one-to-one-dana).

permission-enforcement.evidence: Anonymous visitors get 200 for freely/editable/locked notes and a 302 redirect to the index for limited/protected/private notes; signed-in non-owners get 403 on private notes (dana/priya on q4-hiring-plan, admin/priya on one-to-one-dana) and 200 on limited/protected notes. verify asserts the full 8x4 matrix.

permission-labels.evidence: Each editor page renders the permission dropdown (ui-permission) with the seeded state, e.g. 'Private - Only owner can view & edit' on q4-hiring-plan and 'Locked - Only owner can edit' on api-style-guide.

markdown-rendering-variety.evidence: Content covers ATX headings, bullet and ordered lists, task list checkboxes, bold text, inline code, indented code blocks, markdown tables and http links; published views render the same text server-side for assertions.

tables-and-code-blocks.evidence: Tables: onboarding contacts, runbook sign-off, API request rules, hiring bands, postmortem timeline, glossary terms. Code: `yarn dev`, pg_dump, kubectl set image/rollout undo, JSON request and error examples, SQL column references in the postmortem.

tag-chips.evidence: release-runbook and postmortem-dispatch-latency carry visible '###### Tags:' lines (`runbook`, `release`, `incident`, `postmortem`); every seeded history entry also carries fixed tags (onboarding, release, runbook, api, hiring, incident, postmortem, meeting, reference, one-to-one) that populate the /history tag filter.

revision-history.evidence: engineering-onboarding and release-runbook have two revisions each (2026-09-15/2026-11-19 and 2026-10-28/2026-11-20) with distinct fixed content lengths; the other six have one revision at a fixed date. verify compares the revision list (time + length, newest first) for every note.

history-list-per-user.evidence: /history has 7 entries for admin, 5 for dana and 3 for priya with fixed times and titles; admin's list includes q4-hiring-plan but not one-to-one-dana, dana's list includes one-to-one-dana but not q4-hiring-plan. verify compares every entry (title, millisecond time, pinned, tags).

pinned-and-unpinned-history.evidence: engineering-onboarding is pinned in admin's history and release-runbook is pinned in dana's; all other entries are unpinned, so the pinned-first, then newest-first ordering is visible and stable.

guest-authored-note.evidence: platform-glossary was created anonymously (no owner) with the freely permission, so its editor shows no owner and any visitor can edit it.

private-note-isolation.evidence: q4-hiring-plan (admin) and one-to-one-dana (dana) are private: each owner sees an editor, the other signed-in user and anonymous visitors get 403/302 and never see the content, and each appears only in its owner's history.

fixed-timestamps.evidence: Note created/last-change dates (2026-08-11 .. 2026-11-20), revision dates and history times (2026-10-30 .. 2026-11-21) are absolute constants from the seed; two full reset cycles and a re-seed produced byte-identical digests of notes, revisions and history.

reseed-idempotent.evidence: A second ./tester-env seed on a running stack replaced only the eight owned notes and the three users' history; the digest before and after was identical with no duplicate notes or revisions.

reset-reseed-deterministic.evidence: ./tester-env reset && ./tester-env deploy && ./tester-env seed && ./tester-env verify (113 checks) passed twice; the digests of both cycles matched exactly, and ./tester-env verify fails on a freshly deployed stack without a seed.
